title: Vertical transmission, pregnancy, newborn and prophylaxis
guide: Acute→chronic hepatitis→cirrhosis→HCC/liver failure; acute transmission = sexual, per-cutaneous, blood transfusion; vertical (mother to child) with 90% vs 10% chances by HBeAg, developing maximally in the 3rd trimester; antenatal check-up at 28–30 weeks, HBV DNA > 20,000 → start treatment; child after birth: HBIg 0.5 ml + vaccine 0,1,6 with 1st dose within 12 hours; needlestick 6–30% → check anti-HBs (>100 none, 10–100 one booster); sexual contact HBIG 0.06 mL/kg within 14 days; percutaneous/transmucosal HBIG 0.06 mL/kg within 24 hours; vaccine 0,1,6, 1st dose within 1 week; general population 0,1,6 months, 20 μg/0.5 ml, deltoid; CKD 0,1,2,6 months, 40 μg/1 ml, both deltoid double dose.

title: Phases of chronic hepatitis B
guide: Table rows HBeAg, anti-HBe, HBV DNA, ALT; Phase I HBeAg+ chronic infection, immune tolerant, 10–30 years, HBsAg+, HBeAg+, HBV DNA ↑↑, ALT normal → no treatment; Phase II HBeAg+ chronic hepatitis, immune clearance, mildly symptomatic, ALT ↑↑, optimal treatment time; Phase III HBeAg− chronic infection, inactive carrier state, majority population, HBeAg−, HBV DNA lowest; Phase IV HBeAg− chronic hepatitis, inflammation, acute symptoms (fever, malaise, vomiting), ↑ s. bilirubin and liver enzymes; Phase V HBsAg negative chronic infection, no inflammation, minimal fibrosis; acute HBV = anti-HBc IgM +ve vs chronic phase IV confirmed by quantitative HBsAg > 1000 IU/mL, severely symptomatic, very high HBV DNA load.

title: Reactivation risk, clinical features and replicative load
guide: Both markers (HBsAg and anti-HBc IgG) checked before immunosuppressive therapy; HBsAg -ve with anti-HBc IgG +ve reactivates; clinical features split into acute (acute hepatitis B, reactivation) and chronic (asymptomatic presentation, fatigue = most common symptom, fever, rare extrahepatic disease: membranous nephropathy, PAN 30%, arthralgia); cirrhosis assessed with fibroscan; replicative load split into low and high replicative branches, HBeAg +ve with HBV DNA > 20,000 IU/mL (high infectivity, risk of liver injury) and HBeAg -ve precore mutant with HBV DNA > 2,000 IU/mL (anti-HBc reactive, progressive liver injury, bad prognosis).

title: Life cycle, acute hepatitis treatment indications and histology
guide: Sub-genomic mRNA → translation → x-protein → HBxAg (carcinogenic) with host enzyme; pre-genomic mRNA → RNA-dependent DNA polymerase (reverse transcriptase) → DNA → DNA-dependent DNA polymerase → +/- strands → virion/Dane particle; entry via Na-taurocholate (NTCP) receptor; cccDNA forms in the nucleus; note that cccDNA integration with the host genome makes eradication impossible and confers malignancy risk; acute hepatitis treatment indications: S. bilirubin > 3 mg/dl for 4 weeks and INR ≥ 1.5; histology: ground-glass hepatocytes and HBsAg immunohistochemistry with brownish inclusions.

title: Treatment of chronic hepatitis B: thresholds, targets and drugs
guide: Cirrhosis -ve: low infectivity → follow up, otherwise consider treatment; cirrhosis +ve: treatment, decompensated → treatment/transplant; thresholds: HBeAg +ve HBV DNA > 20,000 IU/mL with ALT > 2× ULN, HBeAg -ve HBV DNA > 2,000 IU/mL with ALT > 2× ULN; targets: (HBeAg -ve) seroconversion, ALT normal, suppress HBV DNA; drugs: IFN-α S/c ~30% seroconversion with psychosis, autoimmune thyroiditis, marrow suppression and no role in HBeAg -ve disease, cirrhosis or young Asians; lamivudine good initial response but YMDD mutation resistance and nephrotoxicity; lamivudine + adefovir no significant benefit; tenofovir disoproxil 300 mg OD with proximal RTA and bone mineral disease; entecavir 0.5 mg OD; tenofovir alafenamide DOC and latest, 25 mg OD, fewer side effects.

title: Hepatitis D virus
guide: Delta virus, RNA, with anti-LKM-3 antibody; coinfection = acute HBV + acute HDV, anti-HBc IgM and anti-HDV IgM positive, 5-20% chance of fulminant hepatitis; superinfection (acute on chronic) = chronic HBV + acute hepatitis D, HBsAg and anti-HDV IgM positive, bad prognosis with chronic HDV-related cirrhosis and anti-LKM-3 antibody; closing note: HEV in pregnancy also has a high risk of fulminant hepatic failure.
